det3 HV-scan efficiency: the deck's curve was 12 points low

28 August 2026 · MPGD2026 slide 25 (the HV build) and backups D2a / D2c

The panel was reading CSVs written on 29 June. They plateaued at 81 % where the same chamber, the same night, at the same 490 V reads 93.3 % off its own long run — a 12.5-point contradiction inside one run directory.

Corrected, the plateau is 93–95 % (455–500 V mean 93.5 %), which is det3's published headline. The frame numbers at 560/550/540/530/520 V go 81/78/69/53/~39 % → 94/92/93/90/~90 %.

And there is no low-voltage turn-on. 425 V reads 89.6 %, not 49 %. The gain curve measured on the same sub-runs says why: gain rises exponentially — ×2 every 16.5 V, ×25 across the scan — and even at the bottom the weakest 2 % of muons sit at 9.3 σ, twice the DAQ threshold. The plateau is a gain margin, and what ends it at the top is the discharge rate, not a lack of gain.

What was wrong

Three basis changes landed in July and none of them was ever applied to this scan. Largest term first:

  1. The M3 reference recipe. The old scan is on chi²<5 & NClus≥3 — 2,206 rays on the 490 V sub-run against 938 on the golden chi²<1.0 & NClus=4 (7‑13). A looser reference points worse, and this efficiency is a 5 mm match to it, so the surplus rays land off track and are booked as detector inefficiency. This is most of the 12.5 points.
  2. No significance floor, and pre-reprocessing hits. The matched-filter reprocessing of the raw waveforms (7‑24, ~+40 % hits) and the relative significance floor that makes it usable (apply_significance_floor, rel = 0.10, 7‑25). Without the floor, coherent noise inflates strip multiplicity and pushes ordinary muons over the >50-strip discharge veto.
  3. The active box. The old script took its fixed box from the sub-run with the most reconstructed points — which is the highest-HV one, where >50 % of events are discharges. The discharge cloud blows the box out past the real active area (396.8 mm in y against a 362 mm active height), so rays fall in corners the chamber cannot see. Symptom: has_any reads 95 % there against 99.99 % on the long run.

How it was re-derived

New script mx_june_cosmic_qa/10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py runs every sub-run through the mx_june_wft/02_efficiency.py accounting — the one that produces the deck's 93.5 % — with the box taken from the seed long run, which is the same box the published breakdown uses.

cd mx_june_cosmic_qa
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py sat_det3_1   # 27 June pass 1
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py sat_det3_2   # 27 June pass 2
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py o22_det3     # 22 June, det A
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py o22_det2     # 22 June, det B
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py --compare    # the before/after figure
../.venv/bin/python 10c_hv_scan_gain.py --slides           # the gain curve
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py --radii      # 0.5/1/2/3/5 mm family
../.venv/bin/python 10b_hv_scan_efficiency.py sat_det3_1 --r 1   # one radius, own CSV
../.venv/bin/python 10d_hv_scan_wft_reco.py                # forward fit, 18 sub-runs
../.venv/bin/python 10f_hv_scan_occupancy.py               # threshold-free read pass
../.venv/bin/python 10g_hv_scan_strip_matrix.py            # per-strip significance matrix
../.venv/bin/python 10h_hv_scan_multiplicity.py --slides   # strips over threshold, angle removed
../.venv/bin/python 10e_hv_scan_charge_angle.py --slides   # charge / occupancy / angle + report

Any --r other than 5 mm writes efficiency_vs_hv_r<R>mm.csv beside the published file rather than over it — five other scripts import efficiency_vs_hv.csv by that exact path, and a tighter cut silently replacing it is the same failure mode this whole note is about.

10c refuses to plot before it has checked that the reduction it reads still describes the sub-runs on disk: same sub-run set, nothing re-decoded since the parquet was written, M3 recipe still chi2<1.0 & NClus=4. Given how this whole note started, that check is the point.

Three checks, all passed

checkresult
--closure scores the long run through this exact code and prints it beside the published breakdown exact: 93.131 % vs 93.13 %, and all five categories match
the two interleaved passes (they share no voltage) agree to 1–2 points: 465→94.1 against 460→94.8 and 470→94.9
the independent 22 June scan, other slot, five days earlier now agrees, 91–94 % against 93–95 %
det B on that run, which does have a published breakdown 490 V reads 92.6 % against the published 92.1 %

That third row retires a story the deck was telling. The two scans used to differ by ~10 points, and the gap was explained by the top slot doubling the M3 lever arm into the same fixed 5 mm box. The gap is gone, so the explanation is withdrawn. The lever arm is real and still visible where it belongs — core residual 0.34–0.41 mm in the bottom slot against 0.44–0.59 mm in the top — it simply never cost efficiency at a 5 mm match.

Statistical errors are ~0.9 points and the plateau scatter is a little wider than that, so do not quote a single point to better than ~1.5 points. The collapse at the top is discharges, not gain.

The gain curve

Flat efficiency is the absence of a measurement: it does not say whether the chamber is coasting on a large gain margin or sitting one volt above threshold. So the same sub-runs were reduced a second way, into a gain ladder.

The observable is the threshold-free peak-strip waveform maximum on M3-selected muons — same run, same golden reference recipe, and deliberately no amplitude cut anywhere, because a 5 σ cut would truncate the low tail and bias the low-voltage points up, faking a shallower rise. Because the reference telescope runs at fixed HV and the trigger is external to det3, the same physical population of muons is selected at every voltage; detector inefficiency then shows up honestly as low-amplitude entries rather than as missing events.

estimatord ln A / dV, X [per 10 V]×2 everyunsaturated rangeY view
2nd percentile0.409 ± 0.00517.0 V425–505 V0.407 ± 0.005
10th percentile0.419 ± 0.00416.5 V425–500 V0.415 ± 0.005
25th percentile0.410 ± 0.00316.9 V425–495 V0.411 ± 0.004
median0.414 ± 0.00416.7 V425–490 V0.402 ± 0.004
±1-strip neighbour sum0.422 ± 0.00316.4 V425–505 V0.423 ± 0.004

Ten independent fits spanning nearly a factor of 3 in signal size, and they agree to ±2.5 %. That is the internal check: the spectrum is being rescaled, not reshaped, so the low quantiles are not themselves being dragged by clipping. The neighbour sum is the strongest form of it — the two ±1 strips together carry ~1.1× the peak amplitude here, but their sum only clips once both of them reach the rail, which buys 15 V of headroom — and it lands on the same slope.

Relative only. Nothing here converts ADC to electrons. The DREAM CSA range for the June bench is not recorded, and the Garfield absolute gain is exactly the quantity the T14 campaign found to be ×0.55–0.63 off, so an absolute axis would be a number with no error bar. d ln A / dV is the part that is measured. Restricted to the 460–490 V window where the simulated ladder was run, this same data gives data/sim = 1.52 — the HV-slope test's result, unchanged by anything here.

Read together, the two panels give three numbers that matter for the operating-point argument:

  • At 425 V the gain is 14× below the operating point and the efficiency is still 89.6 %. Whatever sets the plateau, it is not the amount of charge.
  • The weakest 2 % of muons at 425 V peak at 69 ADC — 9.3 σ over the 7.4 ADC pedestal, 1.9× the DAQ's own 5 σ threshold (37 ADC). There is no threshold problem to turn on.
  • Above 500 V the discharge fraction is what moves: 11 % → 54 % of firing events over 500–525 V, while gain keeps doubling every 16.5 V. The high-V edge of the window is a discharge limit, full stop.

How tight a match? 5 mm against 1 mm

Everything above uses the published 5 mm match to the reference. Scoring the same cached events, same box, same denominator at four other radii separates two things the single number hides — whether the chamber saw the muon, and how well it placed it.

match radius0.5 mm1 mm2 mm3 mm5 mm
plateau, 455–500 V [%]26.061.786.591.493.5
425 V [%]19.549.776.083.589.6
525 V [%]14.132.544.247.047.7
A 1 mm curve is not an efficiency curve. The median matched residual is 0.75–0.80 mm across the plateau, so a 1 mm radius cuts inside the residual distribution and the number it returns — 61.7 % — is mostly a containment fraction. Quoting it as a detection efficiency would understate det3 by 32 points. The published 5 mm cut sits at ~6× the residual scale, which is why it is a detection measurement.

What the tight cut does add

The one thing the 5 mm curve cannot see: resolution keeps improving after detection has plateaued. The median residual falls 0.97 → 0.79 mm between 425 and 460 V and then stops, and the 1 mm and 0.5 mm curves rise over exactly that span while the 5 mm curve is already flat. Cross-referenced against the gain ladder, that is ×3.7 in gain bought 0.18 mm of median residual, and the next ×7 in gain bought none. So the low edge of the usable window is set by resolution, not by detection — which is a better reason to stay above ~460 V than the one the deck used to give.

Three caveats on the residual panel, none of which move the efficiency numbers:

  • This is the hits-chain centroid position, the same one the published efficiency uses. For a resolution number the waveform-first wft reconstruction is the better basis (RECONSTRUCTION_BASIS.md); this panel is here to explain the radius family, not to supersede that.
  • The residual contains the reference's own pointing error, 0.224 mm at z = 702 — ~23 % of the variance of the core, real but sub-dominant.
  • The robust core width, 0.40–0.59 mm, is consistent with the published 0.47 mm core at the operating point. The median radial residual is larger (0.79 mm) because it includes the non-Gaussian tail, and it is the median that sets the 1 mm containment.

Past the peak strip: total charge, occupancy, angle

Everything above — the efficiency curve and the gain curve alike — rests on the tallest sample of the tallest strip. That estimator has a hard ceiling: the strip rails at 3872 ADC and above ~500 V essentially every track clips it, so the ladder has to stop exactly where the interesting part begins. It also says nothing about how much of the track the chamber records, or what the extra gain costs the angle.

Three things were added, all on the same M3-golden fiducial population, all on the waveform-first basis: the frozen r06 forward fit over all 18 sub-runs (11,074 events), which censors saturated samples and so keeps measuring where the peak sample cannot; a threshold-free read pass that just sums every sample over ±10 strips (no threshold, no model); and the reduction that puts them together.

The peak-sample gain curve was right — it just ran out of road

estimatord ln Q / dV, per 10 V×2 everyrange
forward-fit charge (deconvolved, rail censored)0.4185 ± 0.002316.6 V425–505 V
raw window sum (no threshold, no model)0.4280 ± 0.002416.2 V425–505 V
peak sample (the gain curve above)0.419 ± 0.00416.5 V425–500 V

Three estimators with nothing in common but the events, agreeing to under 2 %. What saturation cost the peak sample was reach, not accuracy. The ratio (total charge)/(peak sample) is flat to ±5 % up to 500 V and then triples — that is the clipping, made visible.

"×2 every 16.5 V" is an average, not a constant. The local slope between adjacent voltages runs about 0.37 per 10 V over 425–450 V and about 0.50 near 490–500 V, with ±0.05 point-to-point scatter. The ladder interleaves two passes and they agree to 3–5 % where their ranges overlap, so this is curvature and not a pass-to-pass offset. It is ordinary α(E) behaviour — but the doubling voltage must not be carried outside the range it was fitted in.

How much of the track is lit: the depth never changes

The intuition that a low gain should record a shorter track — the far end of the drift column being the most diffused and most attenuated charge, and so the first to go under — turns out to be wrong here, and the forward fit is what shows it.

The fit recovers a charge column of 26.0–28.5 mm (x) and 30.2–34.1 mm (y) against the 30 mm drift gap, with no trend across a factor 29 in charge. At 425 V, 14× down in gain, the whole drift column is still recoverable. (The x/y offset is the estimator — the last depth bin above 5 % of the profile peak — meeting two planes with different sharing, not two different gaps. It is the flatness that carries the result, not the value.)

What does grow is threshold crossing. Strips over 5 σ go 5 → 12 per plane, and the time over 5 σ goes 912 → 1490 ns — but that is nearly twice the 820 ns a muon needs to cross the gap, so it is the resistive/shaping tail emerging from the noise, not more track. Meanwhile the cluster core at 10 % of the peak sits at 5–6 strips at every voltage. The transverse profile is rescaled, not reshaped — the same statement the four parallel quantile lines of the gain curve make about the amplitude spectrum.

Angular resolution: yes, and at the top

Over every fitted plane, s68 against M3 is best at 455 V (1.02°, x) and 460 V (1.06°, y), against 1.15° / 1.21° at 425 V and 1.38° / 1.31° at 515 V. The 3-D opening angle between the reconstructed direction and the ray says it more cleanly: 1.58° at 460 V rising to 2.06° at 515 V, +30 %.

The trap, worth keeping. The fit-quality gate fails on saturated events, and saturated events are the high-gain ones. Gated, the resolution appears to improve to 0.93° at 525 V — while the surviving fraction falls from 100 % to 19 %. Every angle number here is therefore quoted over every fitted plane, and the charge ladder is measured on the ungated (spark-free) set for the same reason.

So the angular optimum sits at the bottom of the efficiency plateau. Efficiency is flat from 455 V; the angle is best at 455–470 V and is 15–30 % worse by 515 V — before the discharge fraction is counted at all. Together with the match-radius result above, both edges of the usable window are now set by something other than detection: resolution at the bottom, saturation and discharge at the top.

Not measured above ~505 V: the window sum clips as well, the 12-strip clusters begin to reach the edge of the ±10-strip summing window, and the spark veto removes 46 % of fiducial rays at 525 V against ~1 % at 425 V. Those points sit in the grey band and enter no fit. The angle numbers are residuals against a reference of finite resolution, with no deconvolution applied, and the charge is relative only — there is no ADC→electron calibration for the June bench range.

Strips over threshold: does low gain lose the small deposits?

The strip count rises steeply with the mesh voltage — 5 → 12 strips over 5 σ per plane across the ladder. Two very different things can do that, with opposite consequences. Either the charge really only reaches threshold on part of the track at low gain, so the faint slices — a strip crossed by a short piece of path, carrying a handful of primary ionisations — drop out, and the low-gain cluster is a broken version of the high-gain one; or the cluster shape is fixed and only its scale moves, so the transverse tails cross the threshold one strip at a time, and the low-gain cluster is the same cluster seen through a higher relative threshold.

The strip count cannot separate them, because it is threshold-limited by construction. What separates them is the amplitude of the strips that did not fire, so a further read pass records every strip in a ±10-strip window in units of that strip's own noise, sub-threshold values kept.

The direct answer: 14–21 % of the charge is invisible at 425 V

The numerator is the charge in cells over 5 σ; the denominator is a threshold-free sum of every sample of every strip in the window. At 425 V that ratio is 85.9 % (x) and 78.9 % (y) of its high-gain plateau, and it closes to within 1 % by 470 V (x) / 475 V (y). So at the bottom of the ladder a sixth of the charge the detector collected never crosses threshold. That is the proposed mechanism, measured.

One bias worth stating. The raw ratio plateaus a few per cent above 1. The denominator is a whole-window sum, so it carries the shaped pulse's undershoot and whatever the 64-channel common-mode median removed from a wide signal — both signal-proportional and negative. That is harmless for the charge slope (a proportional bias cancels in d ln Q/dV, which is why the window sum and the deconvolved fit agreed to 2 %), but it means this ratio is only a detected fraction once it has been referred to its own plateau.

Taking the angle out

A steeper track lights more strips at any gain, and nothing guarantees the sub-runs have identical angle distributions. The M3 telescope supplies the geometric footprint wgeo = gap · |tan θref| / pitch — a reference quantity, so it cannot move with the detector's own gain. Median 4.2 strips in x, 3.5 in y. Fitting nlit = a(V) + b(V) wgeo splits the two hypotheses cleanly: a is the footprint at normal incidence, b is the fraction of the crossed strips that actually fire.

425 Vbest525 V
a, footprint at normal incidence — x2.93—10.74
a — y3.68—12.11
b, strips lit per strip crossed — x0.490.72 @ 460 V0.40
b — y0.400.52 @ 445 V0.40

The rise is almost entirely in a — +7.8 strips in x, +8.4 in y — and it survives angle matching: every wgeo band rises by about the same number of strips rather than in proportion to its width. The count grows because the transverse tail crosses the threshold, not because more track is recovered. And b never reaches 1 at any voltage, which is what dilution predicts: a wider track spreads the same charge over more strips, so its marginal strips are the faintest ones in the event.

The profile rescales; it does not reshape

Per-offset turn-on: the ±1 strip is over threshold in 90 % of events even at 425 V, |k| = 2 crosses 50 % near 445–460 V, |k| = 3 near 470–485 V, |k| = 4 near 510–520 V.

Predicting the count from a fixed shape and a moving threshold

It reproduces the measured multiplicity to within 0.36 strips everywhere between 435 and 490 V. Above 495 V it overshoots by up to 1.7 strips, but that is the measurement being limited — the rail, and up to 34 % of events touching the edge of the ±10-strip window — not the model failing.

Where the mechanism does bite

Dark strips strictly inside the lit span run 3.2 % of the span at 425 V against 0.3 % at 465–470 V, and 13.9 % of x clusters carry at least one hole at 425 V against 2.5 % at best. They are concentrated in the widest footprints — 12.5 % for wgeo > 9 strips — exactly what dilution predicts. The holes at the bottom of the ladder sit at 4.0 σ: strips that just missed, not empty ones.

So both are true, and the split is the useful part. The charge deficit is real and it is not small — 14 % in x, 21 % in y at 425 V — but it is lost from the edges of a cluster whose shape never changes, not out of the middle of the track. And this is the low-voltage half of the angular optimum: at 425 V a seventh of the x clusters are broken and a sixth of the charge is invisible, which is why the angle is worse there than at 455–460 V, where the deficit has closed and saturation has not yet started. The optimum is where those two curves cross.

Cross-check: the strip counts from this pass equal the earlier threshold pass on 22,148 of 22,148 event-planes, maximum difference zero — two separate reads of the same files, same window, same threshold. The caveat no reduction removes: all of this is at 5 σ on the June bench noise. A different threshold moves a(V) bodily and moves the voltage at which the deficit closes. Only the shape result — the profile rescales rather than reshapes — is threshold-free.

The thing to decide before building the slide

There is no efficiency turn-on anywhere in this scan, and that is a real result, not a gap in the data. The chamber is still 89.6 % efficient at 425 V, 65 V below its operating point and 14× down in gain.

It is not an artefact of the new chain either — the gain ladder above is an entirely separate reduction of the same sub-runs, with no reconstruction in it at all, and it puts the weakest 2 % of muons at 425 V comfortably clear of the threshold. The old rise from 49 % to 81 % across 425–455 V was the pre-reprocessing analyzer's amplitude threshold turning on, not the chamber — the same mechanism that moved det4/det6/det7 by 14–21 points in the July reprocessing.

What it does to the argument: it sharpens it. The title "Every volt of gain costs milliseconds" becomes literally true — the volts cost dead time and buy essentially nothing in efficiency across the whole 520–560 V window. The trade is now one-sided in favour of running lower, and the reason we could not go lower was never efficiency. The report's verdict paragraph, which used to call a ~12-point gap "the honest cost of the 540 V decision", is rewritten: both noise placements put 540 V on the plateau and the 540→560 V difference is ~1 point either way.

Three open decisions

  1. The top-left panel is now a flat line. Honest, and much less interesting to look at. Options: keep it; re-scale y to 80–100 % so the ~4-point sag and the high-V collapse are visible (my suggestion, one line in _eff_panel); or drop it from the main flow and let backup D2c carry the bench efficiency.
    ✓ Settled the same evening — and by a fourth option: the panel is a scaled gain curve now. See the next section. _eff_panel is kept and comes back with make_hv_window.py --panel eff.
  2. The extrapolation below 425 V is now nearly horizontal (0.0011 per V, against 0.0141 before). It is a weak statement — the slope times the extrapolated span is smaller than the points' own scatter — and it says only "no turn-on yet by 425 V". It must not be read as a measured plateau below 425 V. Still drawn dashed and labelled.
  3. The bench curve and the run_55 MIP ladder now disagree much more loudly. Over 560→540 V the ladder falls 100→29 % where the bench now says detection went 94→93 %. The existing caveat (the ladder is a reconstructability proxy on a doubles trigger, only its shape is used) is correct but is carrying much more weight.

What the panel became: a gain scale, not an efficiency

Decision 1 above was settled the same evening, and not by any of the three options offered. Dylan: "instead we should show here a scaled gain curve… show the full charge collected, and aim for the peak strip in the median event to be saturated (just barely saturating is probably ideal gain). We'll call this 100 % optimal gain… then we can show percentages of this optimal gain instead of efficiency."

It is the right call for a reason the flat curve makes obvious: a panel that does not move cannot be the left half of a trade whose right half walks 13.9 → 0.9 ms. The efficiency correction stands and matters — but the gain is the quantity the milliseconds are actually being paid for, and the same 27 June scan measures it better than anything else we have.

What 100 % is, and why it is a measurement

The mesh voltage at which the peak strip of the median track just fills the 12-bit sample. That is not modelled: the saturated fraction goes 0.39 at 495 V to 0.66 at 500 V, in both views, so the 0.5 crossing is bracketed by two measured points 5 V apart, at bench 497.0 V (x 497.0, y 497.0 — they agree to 0.04 V).

peak_amp is the tallest sample of the tallest strip in the event — the max strip, which is the thing that clips first, not a per-strip average. It starts clipping in a few per cent of tracks well before the median does:

bench V475480485 490495497500 505510
max strip railed10 %12 %17 % 27 %39 %50 % 66 %80 %94 %

5 % of tracks by 469 V, a quarter by 489 V, half by 497 V, 90 % by 509 V.

"But the gain plot saturates around 500 V" — also right, and a different statement. Half the events have the max strip clipped at 497 V. The median amplitude only reaches the nominal 3871.5 ADC rail near 500 V, because at the 50 % point half the sample is still below it — and 500 V is exactly where the p50 marker visibly lies on the rail line in the gain plot above (67 % of events clipped there, median at 97 % of the rail). That is what the eye reads. Anchoring the scale at 500 V instead of 497 would lower every percentage on it by ~13 %.

The 50 % point barely cares where the clipping line is drawn: 496.4 / 497.0 / 497.1 V for a cut at 0.88 / 0.92 / 0.95 of the rail. A cut at 0.98 gives 508.6 V, but that is no longer a clipping test — per-channel pedestal subtraction spreads the railed population over ~3700–3900 ADC, so it asks whether a channel's rail landed high rather than whether the event clipped. The spark veto is not what sets it either: 496.8 V on the full M3-golden fiducial set against 497.0 spark-free.

What is plotted is the total collected charge, not the peak sample: the deconvolved forward fit censors railed samples and so keeps measuring where the peak sample cannot. Charge and peak amplitude track each other to 1.7 % rms across 445–495 V, so normalising a charge ladder to a saturation voltage is self-consistent.

The mapping — and the mistake in the first version of this figure

Dylan, reading the finished figure: "in my head 560 corresponded to 490, did I have this wrong?" He did not, and checking it turned up a real error in how the curve had been computed.

Only the gas and the site pressure move the voltage, and that is −67.85 V: n_TOF 560 V is read off the bench ladder at bench 492.1 V. Straight out of the blessed equivalence map, the gas term is +72.70 / 72.62 / 72.44 / 72.34 / 72.20 / 71.84 V at 95/5 440 / 460 / 480 / 490 / 500 / 520 V — flat to ±0.4 V — and the pressure term runs −4.84 to −4.34 over the same span. The readout change (CSA 200 → 600 fC) then divides the ADC by three. It is a factor, not a voltage:

pct(W) = Qbench(W − 67.85) ÷ [ 3 × Qbench(497) ]

— and no slope enters it anywhere. The first version folded the factor three into the voltage axis as ln 3 / slope = +26.3 V, one shift of +94.1 V, and evaluated the ladder there. That is exact only for a perfectly exponential ladder, and this one is curved: the local slope runs 0.33 per 10 V near 435–445 V and 0.52 near 485–505. So the slide read the wrong part of the ladder — −13 % at n_TOF 520 V and +6 % at 560 V. The displayed integers moved by at most one point, but the span across the build did not: 4.7× before, 5.7× now.

“the bench equivalent of n_TOF 560 V”shift bench Vwhat it answers
same gas gain+67.9492.1 the plain gas map — where this curve is read
same ADC counts+94.1465.9 …plus the 600 fC CSA, written as volts
same signal-to-noise+102.7457.3 …plus the 23 July noise step — the efficiency map

All three are correct; they answer different questions. The 8.6 V between the last two is exactly ln(9.80/6.85). A rail sits at a fixed number of ADC counts however noisy the channel is, so the noise term has no business in a saturation statement — which is why the efficiency panel's map cannot be reused here.

Full scale of what? It is worth a factor 3

Bench 497 V fills the 200 fC DREAM the scan was taken with. n_TOF ran 600 fC — 3× less ADC per electron — so filling that needs three times the avalanche, at bench ~518 V, n_TOF 586 V. That is why the first version of this figure put 100 % at 518 on the bench axis, which is what Dylan spotted: "on the plot of collected charge vs voltage the 100 % level is at something like 518 V instead of 497 V? Why is this? Can we put 100 % at 497 V instead?"

Both are honest — they answer different questions, and every percentage moves by 3× between them. The 200 fC one is the right lead, for three reasons: it is the scan's own measured saturation point; it leaves nothing on the curve extrapolated (bench 425–505 V covers n_TOF 493–573 V, and the crossing at 565 V is inside it, where 586 V is 13 V past the last trustworthy bench point); and the 600 fC setting was forced by the gamma flash — 668 pC on a single strip, 1113× the DREAM range — rather than chosen for tracking, so referring a tracking gain to it asks for 3× more avalanche than a MIP measurement needs.

The answer

% (raw window sum)12.919.7 30.846.776.4
% if referred to the 600 fC range4.56.8 10.515.926.0

100 % is at n_TOF 565 ± 20 V — just past the top of the build. So we ran at about a third of the gain that fills the readout, and 560 V is at 78 % of it. The ±20 V is the gas map's own bracket: it slides the curve sideways and takes 565 with it, but it does not touch the ratios between setpoints, and the ratios are what the percentages compare.

Linear y axis, on the same request, and it works now where it would not have before: with 100 % at 565 V the drawn range across the build is 14–78 %, where the 600 fC scale ran 4.5–26 and needed a log axis to be anything but a hockey stick. Linear also puts the run-away back on the canvas — the curve is flat-ish to 550 V and then goes vertical, which is the whole argument of the slide.

Withdrawn, from the first version of this section: “nothing on this panel is extrapolated in gain”. On the 600 fC scale that was true of the drawn points and false of the drawn line, and it was only sayable because the +94.1 V form had hidden a 26 V slide along a fitted slope inside what looked like a measured curve. On the 200 fC scale the statement is true again — and this time because the 100 % crossing genuinely falls inside the measurement, not because an approximation concealed where it did not.

Four routes to the same number

The mapping question was worth a full cross-check, so the headline was recomputed by hand and by a route that never touches the forward fit at all — the median peak sample from the independent gain reduction, divided by three for the CSA and referred to the censoring level:

n_TOFthe codeby hand, x by hand, ymedian peak sample ÷ 3
520 V4.53 %4.57 %4.48 % 4.28 %
540 V10.54 %10.68 %10.40 % 10.19 %
560 V25.99 %26.03 %25.96 % 23.14 %

The two views agree to under 1 %, and the peak-sample route — a different estimator, a different reduction, a different saturation definition — lands within 6 % at 520 and 540 V and 11 % at 560 V, where it is itself extrapolating past its last unsaturated point.

The caveat to have ready: "100 % of optimal gain" is a READOUT limit, not a physics optimum. It says the ADC would be full, nothing more. The same scan's angular resolution against M3, over every fitted plane, is best at bench 445–460 V (1.02–1.06°), is already 1.11–1.15° at bench 497 V where the median track saturates, and 1.31–1.38° by 515 V. A resolution is a threshold quantity, so the ledger that carries it across is the signal-to-noise one, putting that optimum at n_TOF 548–563 V — at or a little above where we ran, and well inside the map's own ±20 V. So the scale says how much of the readout's range we were using, not how far from best we were.

Two more limits worth stating. The percentages are gain ratios: there is no ADC→electron calibration for the June bench range, so nothing here is an absolute gas gain. And the flash charge climbs faster with voltage than the cosmic gain does — 0.51 against 0.42 per 10 V over 520–560 V. A 23 % slope difference between a MIP's avalanche and a gamma flash read off a supply current, in different gases and mapped between them, is inside the known scatter, but it is not zero and the imon integration systematic is still open.

The general lesson

A reduction on disk carries no stamp of the chain that made it, and it will keep being plotted long after that basis is superseded — and it gets rationalised rather than caught. Two of this deck's explanations had grown up around the artefact: a slot/lever-arm gap between two scans that actually agree, and a turn-on that is an analyzer threshold. Both had to be withdrawn.

The check that found it in minutes, and which is immune to which chain is "current": a scan point at the operating point must agree with that run's own long-run published breakdown. Then give the re-derivation a --closure mode that scores the published dataset through the new code and prints it beside the published file.

The 29 June originals are kept under <scan>/mx17_3/_superseded_20260629/ with a README saying why, rather than deleted — in case a figure elsewhere turns out to have been built on them.
